phases.message: Mom has been at Oakview since her hospital stay in September, and they're billing her privately because Medicare says she was never really an inpatient. Start in Carenook: read every Saint Ardent stay, the orders, the notes and every notice they gave us.
Saint Ardent's billing portal. Read how each stay was billed and their billing policy. Don't pay a bill an appeal could change.

Myline, Mom's Medicare account; I'm her appointed representative. Read the rules, her record and her claims, then appeal whatever can still be appealed, the right way, so Medicare covers her rehab. She was in a regular room for three nights in March too, so appeal that one if it counts, and the 2024 one if it isn't too late.

Oakview Care. Read her record, the statements, the billing policy and the messages. Then do what protects her while the appeal is decided, and don't pay anything the appeal could change or anyone to file it. Then tell me what you left alone and why.

sa_policy.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026. Saint Ardent Medical Center billing policy. Topics: status-changes, payments.

When a patient's status is changed from inpatient to outpatient observation, the whole stay is billed to Medicare as outpatient (Part B). If Medicare's QIO reverses the change, Saint Ardent rebills the stay to Part A as an inpatient stay: the patient then owes the Part A deductible instead of her Part B share, and the account's balance is recalculated. An account whose stay is under appeal is not final until the QIO decides.
Balances are due on the date shown. No payment is needed to appeal, and nothing goes to collections before 90 days past due.

rules.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026. Medicare's rules for a hospital stay billed as observation, and the appeals that reach it: 42 CFR 405.1210 to 405.1212 (the change-of-status appeal, from the court order in Alexander v. Azar, final rule CMS-4204-F), 42 CFR 409.30 (the qualifying stay for skilled nursing care), 42 CFR 489.20(y) (the MOON) and 42 CFR 405.940 to 405.958 (redeterminations). Topics: observation, counting, status-appeal, how-to-appeal, retrospective, snf-coverage, redetermination, help.

A patient receiving observation services is an outpatient, not an inpatient, whatever room or bed she is in. Only a formal inpatient order makes a patient an inpatient. A hospital must give the Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice (MOON, CMS-10611) to anyone receiving observation services as an outpatient for more than 24 hours, no later than 36 hours after observation begins, or sooner if she is released (the NOTICE Act; 42 CFR 489.20(y)). The MOON explains the status; it is not an appeal notice. When a hospital's utilization review changes an inpatient to outpatient before release, with the physician's agreement, the whole stay is billed as outpatient (Condition Code 44), and the hospital gives a written notice of the change.

Skilled nursing facility care is covered only after a qualifying stay: a medically necessary inpatient hospital stay of at least 3 consecutive calendar days, counting the day of the inpatient admission and not counting the day of discharge, and admission to the skilled nursing facility within 30 days after discharge (42 CFR 409.30). Days as an outpatient receiving observation services, or in the emergency department before an inpatient order, do not count, even overnight.

Since 14 February 2025, a beneficiary in Original Medicare may appeal a hospital's change of her status to the BFCC-QIO when all of these hold (42 CFR 405.1210(a)(3)): she was formally admitted as an inpatient under an inpatient order; the hospital then reclassified her as an outpatient receiving observation services; and either she had no Part B, or she stayed in the hospital 3 or more consecutive days but was an inpatient for fewer than 3, counted as for a qualifying stay. A stay that was observation from the start had no inpatient admission and no change of status to appeal. A stay with 3 or more inpatient days has nothing for this appeal to change. The hospital gives the Medicare Change of Status Notice (MCSN, CMS-10868) to an eligible patient as soon as possible and no later than 4 hours before release.

Expedited: ask the BFCC-QIO, by phone or in writing, before release from the hospital. The QIO decides within 1 calendar day of receiving the records, and the hospital may not bill for the disputed services until it decides (42 CFR 405.1211(b)(1), (c)(6)(i), (e)). Standard: a beneficiary who did not ask before release may still ask the QIO at any time; there is no deadline. The QIO decides within 2 calendar days of receiving the records, and the hospital's billing protection does not apply (405.1211(b)(5), (c)(6)(ii)). The QIO reviews whether the inpatient admission met Part A's criteria. Its decision binds her, the hospital and the Medicare contractor for payment; if it goes against her, she may ask the QIO to reconsider by noon of the day after she is told (405.1212). The request names the hospital's claim, standard or expedited, the date of the inpatient order and the consecutive days in the hospital, counted as for a qualifying stay.

Status changes before the QIO process began (inpatient admissions from 1 January 2009 to 13 February 2025) had a one-time retrospective appeal, filed with CMS's eligibility contractor, not the QIO. Requests had to be received by 2 January 2026. A later request is denied as untimely unless good cause is shown: circumstances beyond the person's control that kept her from filing in time. The QIO's change-of-status review does not cover these stays.

After a qualifying stay, Part A covers up to 100 days of skilled nursing care in a benefit period when she needs daily skilled care: days 1 to 20 at $0, days 21 to 100 at $217 a day in 2026. A benefit period ends after 60 days in a row with no inpatient hospital or skilled nursing care (42 CFR 409.60), and the next inpatient stay starts a new one, with the Part A deductible ($1,736 in 2026). If the QIO reverses a change of status, the hospital stay is covered under Part A as an inpatient stay: she pays the Part A deductible instead of the Part B charges, and the stay can count toward the 3 days.

A redetermination asks the Medicare Administrative Contractor to review a claim's initial determination; it must be asked within 120 days of receiving the Medicare Summary Notice (42 CFR 405.942). A hospital's Part B claim that was paid has nothing denied to redetermine, and a redetermination is not the appeal of a hospital's change of status: that is asked of the BFCC-QIO (42 CFR 405.1211), whose decision binds the contractor.

A QIO review is free, by phone or in writing, and an appointed representative (Form CMS-1696) may ask for it. State Health Insurance Assistance Program counselors help free. No one needs to be paid to file it.

ov_policy.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026. Oakview Care billing policy. Topics: private-pay, medicare-appeals, collections.

When no qualifying inpatient hospital stay is on record, Oakview bills the resident privately: $510 a day from 1 July 2026 ($495 earlier in 2026, $470 in 2024). Personal charges (salon, phone) are never covered by Medicare. Statements are due 15 days after they are issued.

If the resident or her representative has asked, or is asking, Medicare's QIO to review a hospital's change of status, ask us to hold the statement for the days the appeal could cover, and name the appeal in the note; the hold can be asked the same day as the appeal. While a hold is on, that statement is not due, no late fee is charged and it is not sent to collections. If the appeal is won, Oakview bills Medicare Part A for the covered days and refunds or credits anything paid for them; if it is lost, the statement is due 15 days after the decision. A hold is only for a statement whose days that appeal could cover.
A statement unpaid 30 days after its due date, and not on hold, is sent to Corbel Recovery, our collection agency, with a late fee of 1.5%.
